Content: Nonlinear functions take us beyond the world of perfectly straight lines and introduce more complex relationships with curves and changes of direction. While a linear function models things that change at a constant rate, nonlinear functions model scenarios where the rate of change actually changes over time. In the real world, physics and economics are driven by dynamic relationships that aren't necessarily described by straight lines. We can use nonlinear models to calculate the gravity-defying arc of a thrown ball, map the geometric spread of a viral video on social media, or determine the optimal price of a product to maximize sales.

On the SAT exam, it's very useful to understand nonlinear functions — specifically quadratic functions — since they are a key component within the Advanced Math category. Quadratics are especially common because they have symmetric properties that describe many real-world phenomenon, testing both our geometric intuition and algebraic skills. A `ultext(Quadratic Function)` creates a U-shaped curve on the coordinate plane, so many SAT problems connect mathematical descriptions of a quadratic to the visual features of its graph. For example, we might be tasked with finding the highest or lowest point (vertex) of a quadratic or where it crosses the axes.

To master these problems, we must first understand the concept of a parent function. A `ultext(Parent Function)` is the simplest, most basic version of a family of functions before any extra numbers or operations alter the graph's shape or position. For quadratic functions, the parent function is `y=x^2`. When we graph this parent function, its vertex sits perfectly at the origin `(0,0)`, and it curves symmetrically upward into both the first and second quadrants. Think of the parent function as a mathematical template for quadratics and every complex quadratic as simply a modification of this parent function.

The rules that dictate how this template changes are called transformations. A `ultext(Transformation)` is a minor alteration to the parent function that changes its behavior and appearance. Knowing the different transformation types lets us look at a modified equation and instantly predict exactly how its graph compares to the parent function. These movements include shifts, flips, and stretches that change how the graph looks without changing its overall structure.

:ibox:• `ultext(Shift)`: The position of the graph changes — moving the curve left, right, up, or down — but it keeps the same shape.
• `ultext(Reflection)`: The graph is flipped vertically or horizontally which changes the orientation of the curve. Vertical reflections flip a quadratic function upside down so it faces downward like a frown. Horizontal reflections don't change the shape of a quadratic curve due to their symmetry, but will change their position to a different quadrant if there is already a shift to the function.
• `ultext(Dilation)`: The graph is stretched or compressed without changing direction or position, meaning the curve either becomes more narrow or flattens out and becomes wider.

Understanding parent functions and transformations lets us identify how changes to a quadratic function affect the features of its graph. Without needing to plug in coordinate points to test an answer choice, we can translate the description of transformations into the visual characteristics of a curve. By understanding difference between a quadratic function and the parent function, we can bypass tedious calculations and identify the correct equation or graph.
